newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Cor Boonstra - set to stir already shaken Philips.
newsitem.headline: Cor Boonstra - set to stir already shaken Philips.

text.p: When Cor Boonstra becomes the new chairman of Philips Electronics on Tuesday he will be the first outsider in the firm's 105-year history to head the company and that could be what brings him success.
Boonstra, who only joined the Eindhoven-based company in 1994, replaces Jan Timmer who hauled Philips back from the brink of financial disaster after big losses in the early 1990s.
Timmer blasted Philips out of a decades-long complacency, forcefully reminding managers and workers alike that they had to listen to what their customers wanted and deliver it quickly.

But while Philips is no longer in intensive care it is still seen as limping along in international markets -- a little unfocused, not quite as competitive as the Japanese, some parts doing well and others just not living up to their potential.

Boonstra, a former president of U.S. consumer products giant Sara Lee Corp, could be the man to sort that out, say analysts, bringing a new shot of the killer instinct needed to make the world sit up and take notice of Philips' brands.

"He's not a Philips man. Maybe it brings a fresh approach. He's come from a background at Sara Lee that's strong on brand names, pretty good on restructuring -- all things that are relevant for Philips," said London-based Angela Dean of brokers Morgan Stanley.
His stewardship at Sara Lee caused eyebrows to rise and sparks to fly as he hacked back jobs and costs, prompting mutterings about his aggressive, no-holds-barred style.
"We all know he's a man in a hurry," said one Philips insider, "He's 58 now and he's due to retire at 62 so he hasn't got that long to get some results."

And some at Philips believe this might be a telling factor in Boonstra's administration, leading him to come up with tough new measures that might make Timmer, nicknamed "Hurricane Gilbert" for the impact he had on Philips, look positively mild.
Philips insiders say Boonstra believes Jan Timmer took time to persuade people, to educate them that their cosy ways of doing things were leading nowhere before taking action.
That might have been a luxury, they say and workers under Boonstra will have to show market savvy and shape up fast, identifying new products and markets.
"He has a well known style that he's somebody with a short fuse, if things can't be solved in the forseeable future they have to change," said Eric de Graaf of ING Barings.
The tall, slim Boonstra is said to have the same aggressive instincts as his stocky, bullet-headed predecessor Timmer, and is likely to prove an exacting boss.
"He is a man who expects people to live up to their commitments, to produce what they say they will -- that's how HE does things," said the Philips source.
Boonstra, the son of a grocery store owner, was born and bred in commerce -- learning the value of teamwork in hours put in after school working in his father's shop.
The background he shares with Britain's former prime minister Margaret Thatcher gives him similar views on self reliance and industriousness, say insiders.
It probably also gives him the force of character to push through tough job cuts at Philips in the Netherlands, moving production to cheaper venues if he has to.
He made his first independent guilder at the age of 10 buying up flowers at wholesale prices and then reselling them in his hometown in the northern province of Friesland.

And later, while other children spent a traditional school-free Wednesday afternoon at play, the young Boonstra was plying the streets on his bike, selling margarine to housewives and dreaming of joining the navy.
Although turned down by the navy because of his eyesight, Boonstra showed the fierce streak of independence for which he is known by quitting school and joining the merchant marine.
He speaks warmly of creating wealth, and is known to admire the enterprise culture of Asia where workers are prepared to put in long hours to achieve higher standards of living.
Married with four children, Boonstra lives in Antwerp in Belgium, an hour or so's car ride from Philips' Eindhoven headquarters and at the heart of the Benelux region.
He describes himself as a sociable man, definitely not a loner, whose main interests in what little leisure time he has are sailing and jazz music.
